The molecular split shares all 2,221 SMILES classes across training, validation, and test conformers. Thus Θ and Λ may learn or memorize class-specific distributions; there is no molecule-disjoint or unseen-symmetry evaluation supporting the claimed generalization to unseen inputs.

These are not generally the intrinsic Riemannian Fréchet mean analyzed in the theorem, and the SO(3) normalization formula also omits the claimed inverse.

The theory assumes i.i.d. samples from an exact equivalence class, whereas the algorithm uses a local k-nearest-neighbor set. This set is neither the connected-component equivalence class defined in the paper nor an i.i.d. class sample, so the theorem does not justify the actual procedure. Architecture-agnosticism is also not demonstrated beyond an IE-AE backbone.

The evaluation is predominantly synthetic and class-conditioned: rotations are injected according to digit labels or one of only three matrix-Fisher matrices. Train and test splits share digit classes and molecular identities, so the experiments do not establish generalization to unseen classes, molecules, or naturally occurring instance-specific pose distributions.

Evidence for the central symmetry-recovery claim lacks strong quantitative baselines. The closest method, SGM, is compared only qualitatively; there are no simple constant, supervised-oracle, alternative density-estimation, or additional class-pose baselines. The raw matrix-parameter MSE and visually selected threshold of 800 make the claimed 80% SO(3) success rate difficult to interpret.

Several evaluation and reproducibility problems remain: EquiAdapt and ESCNN hyperparameters are explicitly selected using test accuracy; the FashionMNIST OOD protocol refers to symmetry ranges that are never defined; the GEOM downstream classification target is unspecified; uncertainty estimates and numbers of runs are unclear despite a stated fixed seed; and the promised repository URL is absent.

The OOD experiment calls midpoint-distance heuristics negative-log-likelihood scores even though a uniform density has constant likelihood within its support, and the two proposed heuristics are not equivalent up to a constant. This weakens the interpretation of the centering comparison.

The 'plug-and-play, retrain-free' framing is overstated: although the downstream predictor is frozen, RECON requires training an IE-AE plus two sizeable predictors, reportedly taking up to roughly 7.5 GPU-days. On GEOM-QM9 the gain is modest and remains far below the equivariant model and perfect-canonicalization references.

Proposition 3.1 largely packages standard equivariance and consistency facts, while the proposed Tukey-Fréchet construction is an application of established robust M-estimation rather than a well-developed new estimator.

The claimed “natural pose” is defined by the selected centering functional rather than identified from data in a semantic or physically privileged sense. For multimodal distributions and inputs with stabilizers, the center can be non-unique. The Tukey objective merely selects one mode according to initialization or sampling noise, so consistent canonical orientation across classes is not guaranteed.

The main proposition omits important assumptions needed by its proof, including uniqueness of Fréchet means, appropriate support/curvature and moment conditions, and the local conditions under which the mean map is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance. It also assumes exact pose equivariance. Moreover, the theory samples from a true equivalence class, whereas the implementation uses a fixed-size k-nearest-neighbor set with possible contamination; no finite-sample or k-NN consistency result connects the two.

There is a substantial theory-to-implementation mismatch. The image experiments use the ordinary circular mean, while the SO(3) experiments estimate a matrix-Fisher mode via moment matching; neither implements the highlighted Tukey-Fréchet estimator. The experiments do not convincingly demonstrate discovery of unknown real-world symmetries. MNIST and FashionMNIST receive label-conditioned synthetic rotations, while molecular conformers are explicitly aligned and then assigned one of only three artificial matrix-Fisher distributions. Thus the “large-scale, real-world 3D” framing overstates what is evaluated.

The molecular split is especially weak evidence of generalization: conformers are split within each molecule, so every test molecule identity is represented during training, and its randomly assigned rotation distribution is constant across splits. The invariant predictor can therefore memorize molecule-to-distribution assignments. There is no evaluation on held-out molecule identities or genuinely unseen symmetry profiles.

Key comparisons and ablations are missing. The closest SGM method is not evaluated quantitatively; the claimed class-pose-backbone agnosticism is tested only with IE-AE; and there are no simple geometric alignment, PCA/moment, template-matching, test-time augmentation, or prediction-averaging baselines. Parts of the evaluation protocol are invalid or under-specified. EquiAdapt and ESCNN hyperparameters are explicitly selected by test accuracy. Seed counts are unclear, molecular accuracy reports effectively zero variance, and the SO(3) claim that roughly 80% of cases are accurate relies on a visually chosen MSE threshold rather than a principled distributional metric.

weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited. Given an equivariant pose map ψ(x)=gΓ, estimating Γ by a location statistic and right-translating by Γ^{-1} is a straightforward gauge-fixing operation. Moreover, the target distribution is defined to have identity Fréchet mean, making much of the recovery result true by construction rather than establishing recovery of an independently identifiable natural pose.

Proposition 3.1 is not valid at its stated level of generality. Fréchet means need not be unique, and the proof invokes strict geodesic convexity and Lipschitz continuity without assuming convex-support, curvature, or uniqueness conditions. It also requires a right-invariant metric without stating this, mixes a general metric space with additive norm-bounded noise, and does not rigorously justify the final Wasserstein convergence. The practical k-nearest-neighbor sets are not the equivalence classes or i.i.d. class samples assumed by the theorem.

A G-equivariant map ψ:X→G cannot exist on inputs with nontrivial stabilizers: if hx=x, equivariance implies ψ(x)=hψ(x), hence h=e. Likewise, a truly G-invariant η cannot distinguish two inputs that are exactly related by G. This conflicts with the claims about symmetric inputs and distinguishing group-related classes such as 6 and 9; the experiments can succeed only through deviations from exact group orbits.

The robust Tukey-Fréchet discussion is unsupported. Symmetric multimodal distributions have multiple equally valid Tukey minima, so initialization merely introduces another arbitrary reference and cannot identify a unique principal mode. The claim that the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean on SO(2) is generally the circular mean is also incorrect. More importantly, the experiments do not implement the proposed robust estimator: they use a circular mean for SO(2) and a fitted matrix-Fisher mode for SO(3), neither of which is the analyzed estimator.

The evidence for instance-specific symmetry discovery is weak. All pose distributions are synthetically imposed; MNIST/FashionMNIST use only two or three class-level parameter settings, and every molecule is assigned one of only three matrix-Fisher templates after explicit alignment. Train and test splits retain the same digit and molecule identities, so Θ can largely recognize or memorize an identity and output its template. There are no unseen-class tests or simple clustering, nearest-neighbor, constant-template, or supervised-oracle baselines.

The GEOM evaluation is particularly under-specified: the downstream classification target is never stated, no aggregate distributional metric or meaningful baseline accompanies the matrix-Fisher MSE, and the claim that roughly 80% of molecules are accurate relies on an ad hoc MSE<800 threshold selected from visual inspection. Calling this recovery of real-world molecular symmetries is misleading because the evaluated orientations were synthetically sampled.

The experimental protocol has validity issues. The manuscript reports error bars while simultaneously saying that all runs use one fixed seed, without specifying the number or source of repetitions. OOD evaluation compares only against an internally constructed IE-AE variant on synthetic anomalies.

The plug-and-play and no-retraining language is overstated: although the downstream predictor is frozen, RECON requires training a domain-specific IE-AE plus two additional networks, taking about 7.5 A100-days for GEOM, and requires G to be specified in advance. Generality is shown only for one class-pose backbone and compact rotation groups.
